# DNA automaton (Benenson-Shapiro)

`dna-automaton` · *Shapiro 1998-1999 (blueprint); Benenson, Paz-Elizur, Adar, Keinan, Livneh & Shapiro 2001 (first automaton); Benenson, Adar, Paz-Elizur, Livneh & Shapiro 2003 (the ATP-free automaton implemented here)*

*Also known as:* *molecular finite automaton*, *DNA finite-state machine*, *autonomous molecular computer*, *doctor in a cell*

## Introduction

The DNA automaton is a small computer made of molecules that runs by itself in
a test tube. It was built in the laboratory by Ehud Shapiro's group at the
Weizmann Institute: a first version by Benenson, Paz-Elizur, Adar, Keinan,
Livneh and Shapiro (2001), and the ligase-free version that Chemart models by
Benenson, Adar, Paz-Elizur, Livneh and Shapiro (2003). It is a wet-lab
experiment, not a simulation model. Chemart's entry is the reaction network of
that experiment, written with the real DNA sequences.

What it computes is a **finite automaton**, the simplest kind of machine in
computer science. A finite automaton reads a string of symbols from left to
right, one at a time. At each moment it is in one of a few *states*, and a
table of *transition rules* says, for the current state and the symbol just
read, which state to go to next. When the string is used up, the final state is
the answer. The automaton the paper uses as its example has two states, `S0`
and `S1`, reads strings over the letters `a` and `b`, and answers the question
"does the string contain an even number of `a`s?". It starts in `S0`, switches
state at every `a`, ignores every `b`, and accepts the string if it ends in
`S0`. On `abba` it goes `S0 → S1 → S1 → S1 → S0`: two `a`s, accepted.

In the test tube, the string is a double-stranded DNA molecule, each rule is a
short DNA molecule (the *software*), and the machine that applies the rules is
one enzyme, FokI (the *hardware*). FokI binds a fixed DNA sequence and cuts the
DNA a fixed distance away from it. Each cut removes one symbol from the front
of the input and exposes the next one, marked with the new state. The three
kinds of molecule are mixed once, and the computation runs to the end with no
further intervention. The 2003 version needs no external energy either: the
chemical energy released by cutting the input's own backbone drives each step,
so the input is "both data and fuel", as the paper's title puts it.

The project grew out of a more ambitious plan. In 1998 Shapiro designed and
patented a molecular Turing machine, an enzyme-like device that would read,
rewrite and move along a polymer tape. It was presented in 1999 but published
only in 2012 (Shapiro 2012). The book reports that building it proved too
difficult for lack of sufficiently specialised enzymes, so Shapiro and Benenson
started with the simplest possible machine, a two-state automaton (book
§19.3.1).

Banzhaf and Yamamoto present it in their chapter on wet artificial chemistries,
right after [Adleman's DNA Hamiltonian path computation](dna-hpp.md). The two
make a contrast. In Adleman's experiment the DNA strands assembled candidate
answers by themselves, but extracting the right one needed human intervention
at many steps, and the whole procedure took about a week; the automaton runs
autonomously once mixed. The same automaton appears a second time in the
catalog, re-expressed as string-rewriting rules, as the default system of
[Tominaga's stacked-string chemistry](tominaga-stacked-strings.md); that entry
is an abstract rewriting model, while this one keeps the published molecules
and concentrations. The book also notes that [Fraglets](fraglets.md), a
chemical programming language for network protocols, works like the automaton
in one respect: rules act only on the front of a molecule, digesting it from
the front.

## How it works

### Symbols, and how a sticky end carries the state

A DNA double strand (a *duplex*) is two complementary strands, conventionally
called *sense* and *antisense*, each read in its chemical direction, from the
5′ end to the 3′ end. When one strand overhangs the other by a few bases, the
single-stranded overhang is a *sticky end*: it can pair (*hybridise*) with any
other sticky end whose bases are complementary.

In the input molecule each symbol is a 5-base-pair (bp) block of duplex:
`a = TGGCT`, `b = GCAGG`, and a terminator `t = GTCGG` that marks the end of
the string. Neighbouring symbols are separated by a 3-bp spacer, `GCC`. The
front of the molecule ends in a 4-base sticky end cut out of the first
unprocessed symbol, and *which* four of its five bases are exposed encodes the
state:

- the leftmost four bases mean state `S1` (for `a`, `TGGC`);
- the rightmost four bases mean state `S0` (for `a`, `GGCT`).

So a single 4-base sticky end reads as a pair <state, symbol>, and there are six
of them: <`S0`, `a`>, <`S1`, `a`>, <`S0`, `b`>, <`S1`, `b`>, and the two for
the terminator. A fresh input starts in `S0`: it is made with its first symbol
already trimmed to the `S0` window.

### FokI and the software molecules

FokI is a restriction enzyme, a protein that cuts DNA. It recognises the
sequence `GGATG` and cuts 9 bases further along on one strand and 13 bases
further along on the other. The staggered cut leaves a new 4-base sticky end.

A software molecule is a short duplex with three parts, read towards the input:

1. a 4-base sticky end (the *detector*), complementary to one <state, symbol>
   pair, so that it pairs only with an input showing that pair;
2. the FokI site `GGATG`;
3. a *spacer* of 0, 1 or 2 bp between them.

When the detector pairs with the input, the FokI bound to the software molecule
cuts the input 9 and 13 bases from its site. The spacer shifts where that cut
falls inside the input, and therefore which window of the *next* symbol ends up
exposed: a 0-bp spacer moves the machine from `S1` to `S0`, a 1-bp spacer keeps
the current state, and a 2-bp spacer moves it from `S0` to `S1`. The eight
possible rules of a two-state, two-symbol automaton (two states × two symbols ×
two next states) are the eight published software molecules `T1` to `T8`.
Choosing a program means choosing which of them go into the tube.

### One step, from the default network

The default network is automaton A1 (even number of `a`s) run on the published
12-symbol input `abbbbaaaabba`. Its rules are four software molecules:

```
T2: S0 -a-> S1    T3: S0 -b-> S0    T5: S1 -a-> S0    T8: S1 -b-> S1
```

Chemart names an input molecule by its state and the symbols it has left,
terminator included: the starting molecule is `S0_abbbbaaaabbat`. Its sticky
end shows <`S0`, `a`>, which only `T2` detects. The first transition is three
reactions:

```
FokI + T2 -> FokI-T2
FokI-T2 + S0_abbbbaaaabbat -> FokI-T2-S0_abbbbaaaabbat
FokI-T2-S0_abbbbaaaabbat -> FokI-T2 + frag_GGCTGCC_CTGCGGC + S1_bbbbaaaabbat
```

1. FokI and the software molecule `T2` assemble into a complex, `FokI-T2`.
   Both steps before the cut are reversible, and Chemart lists each backward
   reaction too (`FokI-T2 -> FokI + T2`).
2. The complex's detector pairs with the input's sticky end, forming a
   *hybrid*. Nothing is chemically bonded yet: the two duplexes are held
   together only by four base pairs.
3. FokI cuts. `T2` has a 2-bp spacer, so the cut on the input's sense strand
   falls 9 − 2 = 7 bases in. Those seven bases, `GGCTGCC`, are the `S0` window
   of `a` plus the `GCC` spacer, and they leave as a small *fragment*, together
   with seven bases of the other strand. The input now starts at `GCAG`, the
   leftmost window of `b`: it shows <`S1`, `b`>. The molecule has become
   `S1_bbbbaaaabbat`, which is exactly the rule `S0 -a-> S1`.

The complex `FokI-T2` comes out of the cut unchanged, ready to process another
input. The next molecule, `S1_bbbbaaaabbat`, is taken up by `FokI-T8`, and so
on, one symbol per transition. After twelve transitions only the terminator is
left. No software molecule detects a terminator, so the computation stops. The
last molecule, here `S0_t`, is the *output*. Its state can be read on a gel from
its length: the labelled strand is 15 bases long for `S0` and 16 for `S1`.

If a program has no rule for the pair an input shows, the computation stops
early on a non-terminator symbol. The automaton is then said to *suspend*.

### Energy and recycling

Each cut breaks two bonds of the DNA backbone (*phosphodiester bonds*, one per
strand). Breaking them releases free energy, and it scatters an ordered string
into loose pieces, which raises entropy. That is what drives the computation
forward: the input is consumed, while FokI and the software molecules are
recycled. In the 2001 automaton each step also joined (*ligated*) the software
molecule to the input with the enzyme ligase, which used up one software
molecule and two ATP molecules per step. The 2003 design dropped ligase, relying
on the finding that FokI can cut across the non-covalent sticky-end hybrid.

### How strongly things bind, and how fast

The paper gives two *dissociation constants* (Kd), the concentration at which a
complex is half dissociated; lower means tighter binding. FokI holds a software
molecule tightly (Kd = 2 nM), while the four-base pairing of software and input
is weak (Kd = 50 µM). It gives no rate constants for these binding steps. What
it measured is the time per transition: about 20 s under the fastest conditions
and 45 s under the conditions that maximise throughput. The reaction volume is
closed, 10 µl at 8 °C, with nothing added or removed during the run.

### Formal specification

Banzhaf and Yamamoto describe every artificial chemistry by three things (book §2.3): the set of possible molecules **S**, the reaction rules **R** that transform them, and the reactor algorithm **A** that decides which reactions happen, and when. For this chemistry:

**S — molecules** (*explicit* — listed up front). DNA duplexes with 4-nt 5' sticky ends, plus the FokI enzyme: the input molecule at every processing stage, the eight transition (software) molecules T1-T8, the FokI-software and FokI-software-input complexes, the scattered symbol fragments and the two output molecules; Species.structure holds the published sequences as 'sense/antisense', each written 5'-&gt;3'

Species ids: FokI, T1-T8, FokI-T&lt;i&gt;, &lt;state&gt;_&lt;remaining symbols&gt;t for an input at a processing stage (S0_abbt, S1_bbt, ..., S0_t for the output), FokI-T&lt;i&gt;-&lt;molecule&gt; for a hybrid and frag_&lt;sense&gt;_&lt;antisense&gt; for a scattered symbol.

**R — reactions** (*explicit* — listed reaction by reaction; molecules per reaction: 1, 2). One transition of the automaton is three reactions (PNAS 2003, fig. 2E): FokI + Ti &lt;-&gt; FokI-Ti (hardware/software assembly, Kd = 2 nM); FokI-Ti + X &lt;-&gt; FokI-Ti-X (sticky-end hybridisation of the software's &lt;state, symbol&gt; detector to the input, Kd = 50 uM); FokI-Ti-X -&gt; FokI-Ti + fragment + X' (irreversible cleavage). FokI binds GGATG and cuts 9 nt downstream on the sense strand and 13 nt downstream on the antisense strand, so the software's 0-, 1- or 2-bp spacer decides which 4-nt window of the next symbol is exposed, i.e. the next state (0 bp: S1 -&gt; S0, 1 bp: keep the state, 2 bp: S0 -&gt; S1). Hardware and software are recycled; the input is consumed and fuels the computation.

No ligase and no ATP: this is the 2003 automaton, which uses FokI's ability to cleave across a non-covalent sticky-end hybrid. In the 2001 automaton each transition also ligated the software to the input and consumed one software molecule and two ATP.

**A — reactor**: `ode` (deterministic rate equations: concentrations change continuously in time); or `ssa` (stochastic simulation (Gillespie): individual reaction events happen at random times).

*How the population is bounded:* none: a closed 10 ul reaction at 8 C in NEB4 buffer

initial_state holds the published concentrations of the chosen `conditions` in micromolar.

### Using it in Chemart

Every parameter at its default:

```python
import chemart
net = chemart.generate_network("dna-automaton", seed=1)
print(net.summary())
```

```
dna-automaton: 40 species, 44 reactions, status=complete
provides: initial-state, mass-conservation, stoichiometry, topology
seed: 1
extras: analysis, conditions, conservation, published
```

Its first reactions (`net.reactions`):

```
FokI + T2 -> FokI-T2
FokI-T2 -> FokI + T2
FokI + T3 -> FokI-T3
FokI-T3 -> FokI + T3
FokI + T5 -> FokI-T5
FokI-T5 -> FokI + T5
FokI + T8 -> FokI-T8
FokI-T8 -> FokI + T8
… and 36 more
```

The default call builds the network for one lane of the paper's fig. 3B:
automaton A1 on input I8 (`abbbbaaaabba`), at that figure's concentrations (in
micromolar, in `net.initial_state`). It has 4 software molecules and 12
transitions, so 2 × 4 assembly reactions plus 3 × 12 transition reactions: 44
in all. What happened is in `net.extras["analysis"]`:

```python
a = net.extras["analysis"]
a["program"], a["decides"], a["accepting_state"]
# ('A1', 'the input contains an even number of a symbols', 'S0')
a["transition_table"]
# {'T2': 'S0 -a-> S1', 'T3': 'S0 -b-> S0', 'T5': 'S1 -a-> S0', 'T8': 'S1 -b-> S1'}
run = a["runs"][0]
run["final_state"], run["accepted"], run["output"], run["output_antisense_nt"]
# ('S0', True, 'S0_t', 15)
a["transitions_per_software_molecule"]
# {'T2': 3, 'T3': 0, 'T5': 3, 'T8': 6}
net.initial_state
# {'FokI': 4.0, 'T2': 1.0, 'T3': 1.0, 'T5': 1.0, 'T8': 1.0, 'S0_abbbbaaaabbat': 1.0}
```

Each entry of `run["transitions"]` records one step (`transition`, `from`,
`symbol`, `to`, `molecule`, `product`). Every species carries its DNA in
`Species.structure` as `sense/antisense`, both 5′→3′. `net.extras["published"]`
holds the paper's measured numbers (fidelities, throughput, energetics, the Kd
values), which the network itself cannot express. `net.extras["conservation"]`
gives a nucleotide count per species, conserved by every reaction.

Species names: `FokI`; `T1`…`T8`; `FokI-T2` for a loaded enzyme;
`FokI-T2-S0_abbt` for a hybrid; `S1_bbt` for an input in state `S1` with `bb`
and the terminator left; `frag_<sense>_<antisense>` for a cut-off symbol.

The network has no rate on any reaction by default, because the paper gives no
step time for fig. 3B. The generator returns the network and the outcome of
each run; it does not follow concentrations through time. To simulate the
network with rate equations or a stochastic solver you would also need rates
for the binding steps, which the paper does not publish.

**The whole of fig. 3B.** The three programs on the eight published inputs:

```python
inputs = ["I1", "I2", "I3", "I4", "I5", "I6", "I7", "I8"]
for program in ("A1", "A2", "A3"):
    net = chemart.generate_network("dna-automaton", program=program, inputs=inputs)
    print(program, " ".join(f"{r['input']}:{r['final_state']}"
                            for r in net.extras["analysis"]["runs"]))
```

```
A1 I1:S1 I2:S0 I3:S0 I4:S1 I5:S0 I6:S1 I7:S1 I8:S0
A2 I1:S1 I2:S0 I3:S1 I4:S0 I5:S1 I6:S0 I7:S1 I8:S0
A3 I1:S1 I2:S0 I3:S1 I4:S0 I5:S1 I6:S0 I7:S1 I8:S0
```

A2 decides "even number of symbols" (accepting `S0`) and A3 "ends with `b`"
(accepting `S1`). All eight inputs go into one network (the A1 network has 115
species and 146 reactions), whereas in the paper each lane was a separate tube;
molecules that two inputs pass through are one species. The three calls take
about 1.5 s together.

**The book's automaton.** `program="book"` builds the automaton of the book's
fig. 19.13, which accepts an even number of `b`s (rules `T1`, `T4`, `T6`,
`T7`). It is a legal program, but it was not among those run in the lab. On I1
to I4 it accepts `abb` and `abba` and rejects `babbabb` and `babbabba`.

**Your own program and input.** `transitions` takes any set of software
molecules, `accepting_state` its accepting state, and `inputs` also takes
literal strings over `a` and `b`. A program without a rule for some pair
suspends:

```python
net = chemart.generate_network("dna-automaton", transitions=["T2", "T5"],
                               inputs=["ab", "aa"], accepting_state="S0")
```

gives, for `ab`, `final_state='S1', suspended=True, unprocessed='b'` (no rule
for <`S1`, `b`>), and for `aa`, `final_state='S0', accepted=True`. Two software
molecules that detect the same pair, such as `T1` and `T2`, are rejected with a
`ValueError`, since the model covers only deterministic automata. Long inputs
are cheap: a 1,000-symbol input builds in about 1.3 s.

**Published rates.** `conditions="fast"` and `conditions="parallel"` put the
measured step time on every cleavage reaction as a mass-action constant,
k = 1/20 s = 0.05 s⁻¹ and k = 1/45 s ≈ 0.0222 s⁻¹, and set the concentrations
of those experiments. Both experiments used program A2 on input I3, but the
conditions do not select them, so ask for them explicitly:

```python
net = chemart.generate_network("dna-automaton", program="A2", inputs=["I3"],
                               conditions="fast")
net.initial_state
# {'FokI': 4.0, 'T2': 1.0, 'T4': 1.0, 'T5': 1.0, 'T7': 1.0, 'S0_babbabbt': 0.01}
```

**Software reuse.** `conditions="reuse"` sets the fig. 3C concentrations (A1 on
I8, each software molecule at 0.075 µM against 1 µM input, 1 µM FokI). With the
default program and input, that is the fig. 3C experiment.

#### Parameters

Pass any of these as keyword arguments to `generate_network`. The *role* column says what a parameter controls: `structural` (which molecules and reactions exist), `kinetic` (rates), `thermodynamic` (energies, temperature), `population` (sizes, budgets, initial state), `spatial`, `stochastic` or `selection`. *range* gives the values used in the published work.

| name | type | default | role | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `program` | `enum` | `A1` | structural | which automaton to build: A1 (even number of a symbols), A2 (even number of symbols) and A3 (ends with b) are the three programs run in PNAS 2003 fig. 3B; book is the even-number-of-b automaton of book fig. 19.13, which was not run in the lab <br>one of `A1`, `A2`, `A3`, `book` · *range:* ignored when `transitions` is given |
| `transitions` | `list` | `[]` | structural | explicit program as a list of published transition-molecule names (T1: S0-a-&gt;S0, T2: S0-a-&gt;S1, T3: S0-b-&gt;S0, T4: S0-b-&gt;S1, T5: S1-a-&gt;S0, T6: S1-a-&gt;S1, T7: S1-b-&gt;S0, T8: S1-b-&gt;S1); overrides `program`. Two molecules detecting the same &lt;state, symbol&gt; are rejected <br>*range:* any of the 2^8 subsets that is deterministic; the book notes that all eight transitions of a two-state two-symbol FSM are realisable |
| `accepting_state` | `enum` | `S0` | structural | accepting state, used only with an explicit `transitions` program; the named programs carry their published accepting state (S0 for A1, A2 and book, S1 for A3) <br>one of `S0`, `S1` |
| `inputs` | `list` | `['I8']` | population | input molecules, given as published input names (I1 abb, I2 abba, I3 babbabb, I4 babbabba, I5 baaaabb, I6 baaaabba, I7 abbbbabbabb, I8 abbbbaaaabba) or as literal strings over {a, b}; each one is added to the same reaction at the concentration of `conditions` <br>*range:* fig. 3B runs each of I1-I8 in a separate tube |
| `conditions` | `enum` | `standard` | kinetic | which published reaction sets the concentrations and the per-transition rate: standard (fig. 3B: 1 uM input, 1 uM of each software molecule, 4 uM FokI; no rate published), fast (10 nM input, 20 s per transition), parallel (5 uM input, 2.5 uM of each software molecule, 10 uM FokI, 45 s per transition, 6.646e10 transitions/s/ul) and reuse (fig. 3C: software at 0.075 molar ratio for 18 h; no rate published) <br>one of `standard`, `fast`, `parallel`, `reuse` |

### Implementation decisions

The sources leave gaps, and sometimes contradict each other or the book. Each such case, and how Chemart resolved it, is listed here: read these before quoting a number from this page.

??? note "13 decisions"

    - Attribution: the book's refs for this entry are [767] = Shapiro (2012, Interface Focus, the mechanical Turing machine blueprint), [768] = Shapiro & Benenson (2006, Scientific American) and [100] = Benenson et al. (2003, PNAS). The book itself says 'a detailed description of the DNA automaton can be found in [100]', and figs. 19.14-19.16 cite [100]. The implementation therefore follows the 2003 PNAS automaton, not the 2001 Nature one, and the 2001 paper (which the bibliography does not list under this entry) is recorded in sources as the original.
    - The 2001 automaton ligated each software molecule to the input, consuming one software molecule and two ATP per transition (1000 s per transition). Its sequences are only in the paywalled Nature paper, so only the 2003 ATP-free design - the one the book's figures show, with the software recycled and the input as the only fuel - is implemented.
    - Every transition rule is derived from the published oligonucleotides rather than typed in: the 4-nt 5' antisense overhang gives the detected &lt;state, symbol&gt; (its reverse complement is that symbol's S1 window if it is the leftmost four bases, its S0 window if it is the rightmost four), and the number of sense bases between GGATG and the end of the software duplex (0, 1 or 2) gives the next state. The eight rules so derived reproduce fig. 2C exactly (test).
    - Book fig. 19.13 shows a two-state automaton that accepts an even number of b symbols, while the automaton of PNAS fig. 1A (A1) accepts an even number of a symbols. Both are implemented: A1-A3 are the three programs actually run in the lab, `program: book` is the book's example, which was not.
    - Input molecules are reconstructed from the encoding (5-bp symbols a = TGGCT, b = GCAGG, terminator = GTCGG, 3-bp spacer GCC, 4-nt 5' sense overhang encoding &lt;S0, first symbol&gt;, 1-nt 3' A extrusion). The reconstruction reproduces the published abb and abba oligonucleotides base for base, and I3-I8 reproduce the published ligation products of the blocks babb2, baaa2 and abbb3 (test).
    - Species are deduplicated by molecule, not by input: an intermediate is fully determined by &lt;state, remaining symbols&gt;, so two inputs that reach the same configuration share the species. All inputs listed in `inputs` sit in one reaction volume; in fig. 3B each lane was a separate tube.
    - The scattered symbol is kept as one species, a 7-9 nt duplex with 3-5 bp paired, exactly as cleaved. The paper says it probably dissociates into single strands in solution; that dissociation, and the reversible rebinding of fragments to sticky ends that it mentions for very long inputs, are not modelled.
    - Rates: only the measured per-transition times are used, as a mass-action constant on the cleavage step (k = 1/20 s for `conditions: fast`, k = 1/45 s for `parallel`), with the conditions recorded on the rate dict. The published Kd values (2 nM hardware/software, 50 uM software/input) are equilibrium constants, not rate laws, so the assembly and hybridisation steps carry no rate and the Kd values are recorded in extras['published']. The default `conditions: standard` (fig. 3B) has no published step time and therefore no rate constant; `provides` claims rate-constants for the fast and parallel conditions.
    - The computation stops when the exposed sticky end encodes the terminator, which no software molecule detects; the remaining molecule is the output, with a 15-nt antisense strand for S0 and 16 nt for S1, the two bands of the published gels. A program that has no rule for some exposed &lt;state, symbol&gt; suspends, and the run is marked suspended in extras['analysis'].
    - Nondeterministic programs (two software molecules detecting the same &lt;state, symbol&gt;, i.e. the stochastic computing of Adar et al. 2004) are rejected with a ValueError: the network here is the deterministic cascade.
    - The hardware/software complex is recycled over a cycle, not within a reaction: the hybridisation step consumes it and the cleavage step releases it, so no reaction has a species on both sides and the `catalysts` capability is not claimed. The tests check the cycle instead.
    - The generator is deterministic: `rng` is unused and the seed does not change the network.
    - v1 params dropped: `automaton` (callable) becomes `program`/`transitions`, `input_string` (matrix) becomes `inputs`, and `n_states` disappears - the FokI construction is fixed at two states (the book notes that larger FSMs would exceed what fits inside FokI).

## Results

All the results below come from Benenson et al. (2003), except where another
source is named.

**Cutting without ligase.** The first finding was that FokI can cut an input
held to its software only by sticky-end pairing, with no covalent bond. Fig. 3A
shows the transition goes ahead whether or not the molecules carry the
phosphate groups that ligase needs, and the software molecule comes out
unchanged. Getting there took redesign. The authors report that long spacers
and sticky ends low in G and C often led FokI to cut only one strand, an
"illegal" configuration, and that short spacers and GC-rich sticky ends worked.
Hence the final design's 0-, 1- and 2-bp spacers, which in turn fixed the symbol
encoding and the spacers between symbols. This is a laboratory control; Chemart
takes the mechanism as given and does not model single-strand cuts.

**Programmability.** Three programs (A1, A2, A3) were run on eight inputs up to
12 symbols long, and in every case the main output band was the predicted one
(fig. 3B). Chemart reproduces this. Its tests check that the transition rule it
reads off each published software sequence matches the paper's fig. 2C, that
all eight two-state, two-symbol rules exist (the book's statement), that the
reconstructed inputs match the published oligonucleotides base for base, that
all 24 program-input pairs end in the expected state, that the output strand is
15 or 16 bases long accordingly, and that the book's automaton counts `b`s.

**Fidelity.** Treating every unexpected gel band as an error (the worst case),
the paper measured a single-step fidelity of 99.9% for input I8 with program A3
and about 99.5% on average for 12-symbol inputs. The error bands did not grow
with input length, so short inputs gave lower apparent values: 95% for A1 on
the four-symbol I2. The authors argue that the real fidelity is higher, since
otherwise 12-step runs would be random, and a separate assay with detection
molecules gave about 99.9% for long inputs, a discrepancy they say they had yet
to explain. Chemart's network is error-free; the numbers are carried in
`extras["published"]` but not modelled.

**Reuse of software.** With software at 0.075 of the input's concentration,
after 18 h the molecules `T2`, `T5` and `T8` had performed on average 29, 21
and 54 transitions each (fig. 3C), so a fixed amount of software processes much
more input than itself. Chemart's network does not track molecule counts over
time. It gives how many times each rule is used per input molecule (3, 3 and 6,
with `T3` unused), and the test checks that `T8` is the most used, as in the
paper.

**Speed and parallelism.** The fastest run (program A2, input I3 at 10 nM)
took 20 s per transition per molecule, about 50 times faster than the 1,000 s of
the 2001 automaton. Maximising throughput instead (5 µM of input I3) gave 45 s
per step and 6.646 × 10¹⁰ transitions per second per µl, about 8,000 times the
2001 figure of 8.3 × 10⁶. The abstract summarises it as 3 × 10¹² automata per µl
performing 6.6 × 10¹⁰ transitions per second per µl. Chemart carries the step
times as rate constants; a test checks that 5 µM corresponds to 3 × 10¹²
molecules per µl, and that dividing by 45 s gives the published throughput to
within 1%.

**Error rate against speed.** The apparent single-step correctness was 98.1%
after 30 s and 98.9% after 4 min in the fast run, a constant 99.5% in the
high-throughput run, and 98.7% after 18 h in the slow recycling run. The authors
conclude that the error rate depends on the molecular structure rather than on
speed. Reaction rates were also similar anywhere between 2 and 20 °C. Not
modelled.

**Energy.** Each transition hydrolyses two phosphodiester bonds, with a
standard free energy change of −44.31 kJ/mol at 25 °C (−41.78 kJ/mol corrected
to 8 °C). For the high-throughput run the paper estimates an average of about
−33.9 kT per transition and at most about 5.3 × 10⁻⁹ W/µl of heat. It compares
the 34 kT with kT ln 2, the theoretical energy of randomising one known bit,
which it is about 50 times larger than. It also points out that the automaton
resembles a low-energy computing device imagined by Bennett in 1973, with the
difference that destroying the input makes it irreversible. These are
properties of the chemistry, not of the network topology; Chemart records them
in `extras["published"]` and does not compute them.

**Later work.** According to the book, Shapiro and Benenson saw in the automaton
a possible route to diagnosis: read its two states as "healthy" and "sick", and
it becomes a "DNA doctor in a cell" (Shapiro and Benenson 2006). Shapiro (2012)
says a 1999 slide with that title was criticised as over-optimistic. The book
lists two extensions: probabilistic transitions (Adar et al. 2004) and automata
that respond to the mRNA levels of disease-related genes (Benenson et al. 2004;
Gil et al. 2011). Chemart implements neither: two software molecules for the
same pair, the basis of the stochastic version, are rejected.

**What is not implemented.** The 2001 ligase automaton is not modelled: its
sequences are only in the Nature paper, which could not be consulted. The book
itself describes the mechanism as using FokI *and ligase*, which is the 2001
design, while its figures (from the 2003 paper) show the ligase-free one that
Chemart follows. The paper suggests that the cut-off fragments probably fall
apart into single strands and, for very long inputs, may slow the computation
by rebinding to sticky ends; neither is modelled. Automata with more than two
states are not offered: the book notes that large automata would exceed what
can be packed into FokI.

### Sources used for the implementation

- Benenson, Y., Adar, R., Paz-Elizur, T., Livneh, Z. & Shapiro, E. (2003). DNA molecule provides a computing machine with both data and fuel. PNAS 100(5):2191-2196. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0535624100, free full text https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC151317/ - the book's reference [100] and the specification used here: figs. 1 (automata A1-A3 and inputs I1-I8), 2 (symbol encoding, FokI, the eight software molecules, the mechanism), 3 (results, software reuse) and Materials and Methods (all oligonucleotide sequences, concentrations, rates, fidelities and energetics).
- Benenson, Y., Paz-Elizur, T., Adar, R., Keinan, E., Livneh, Z. & Shapiro, E. (2001). Programmable and autonomous computing machine made of biomolecules. Nature 414:430-434. https://doi.org/10.1038/35106533 - the original automaton (ligase + ATP, software consumed per step). Paywalled and withdrawn from PMC, so it could not be consulted; it is not implemented here.
- Shapiro, E. (2012). A mechanical Turing machine: blueprint for a biomolecular computer. Interface Focus 2(4):497-503. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsfs.2011.0118 (open access; the book's [767]) - the 1998-1999 blueprint of the molecular Turing machine the automaton was cut down from.
- Shapiro, E. & Benenson, Y. (2006). Bringing DNA computers to life. Scientific American 294(5):44-51 (the book's [768]) - popular account; not used for any number here.
